profile: adjacency matrix: A graph can be coded as a matrix. The adjacency matrix, denoted A, is an N x N matrix that encodes the graph's topology, showing which nodes are adjacent. Different orderings of nodes produce different matrices (Ai and A'i) while preserving the underlying graph topology. Variants such as A_tilde are used. The adjacency matrix is used in graph neural networks and adjacency-matrix-based generative graph neural networks.

graph representation: A graph representation can be written as G=(V,E) or G=(V,E,A,X). Graphs are powerful tools in modeling interactions and relationships between different elements. The learned graph embedding is invariant to its node permutation. Topology is another term associated with graph representation.

road network: A road network is an example of a real-world graph. It appears among objects in a figure of real-world graphs, as part of a discussion of graph types and representations. Road networks are thus an illustrative instance of real-world graphs.
social network: a graph in which nodes represent people and edges represent friendships between them.
citation network: a graph representation of scientific literature. In this graph, nodes are papers and edges are citations.
knowledge graph: A graph where nodes are articles and edges are hyperlinks, as exemplified by Wikipedia.
program flow graph: a graph-based representation of a computer program. In this representation, nodes are syntax tokens, and edges represent computations involving these variables.
geometric graph: a graph representation of a geometric point cloud, where each point is a node and edges connect to other nearby points.
protein interaction network: a graph representation of protein interactions in a cell, where nodes are proteins and edges connect interacting proteins.
hierarchical graph: A representation that can be used to represent a scene.

node embedding: A node embedding is an associated vector representation for each node, often denoted h_k or stored as columns of node data X. It is a latent/hidden representation, also called an encoding or transformation, learned by a graph neural network. Embeddings can be linearly transformed and combined across the graph for graph-level prediction. An example is a five-dimensional vector attached to a node.
edge embedding: a vector representation associated with an edge in a graph; in the illustrated graph representation, each edge has an embedding of length four.
molecular graph: A graph type associated with molecules in a listing of graph types and representations. Molecules are listed as item (b).
circuit graph: Electrical circuits are naturally structured as graphs.

directed graph: A graph type in which edges have an orientation, also called a digraph. The term appears paired with the notation l_ij. It also appears in the context of graph properties and matrix representations.
hypergraph: A hypergraph H is a generalization of a graph in which an edge can join any number of vertices.
hyperedge: A hyperedge is an element of a set of non-empty subsets. In this characterization, the set comprises non-empty subsets, and each hyperedge is itself one of these non-empty subsets.
incidence matrix: a term that appears in the context of graph types and representations.
heterogeneous graph: a graph represented as G = (V, E, R, T).
high-order relationships: High-order relationships are modeled among nodes in graph representations.
weighted graph: A weighted graph is a graph whose edges have associated real-valued weights w_ij. Graphs are categorized as weighted or binary.
node type: In graph representations, a node can have a node type, denoted v_i, where v_i ∈ V.
relation type: A relation type is denoted by r and is an element of a set R.
triplet: a triplet encodes the relationship between pairs of nodes.
edge type: an edge type is the relation type r assigned to an edge in a graph, represented as a triple (v_i, r, v_j) belonging to the edge set E.
simple graph: A graph is simple if it has no loops or multiple edges. This means each edge connects two distinct vertices, and no two edges connect the same pair of vertices.
annotated graph: A graph G is annotated or decorated if its nodes can hold attributes or features.

loop: A loop (also called self-loop or self-connection) is an edge that connects a node to itself. In graph convolutional networks, self-loops are incorporated by modifying the adjacency matrix as A_hat = A + I ('self loop').
multiple edges: two or more edges that connect the same endpoints.

feature matrix: a matrix of node features, typically denoted X and also known as the node feature matrix or input feature matrix. X is equated with H_0 and serves as the input to a graph neural network. The input feature matrix is denoted X^l, and X' also appears in this context. The matrix supplies d features to the GNN block.
embedding matrix: a term appearing in lecture material on graph types and representations and in lecture material on graph neural networks and node embedding.
complete graph: a graph in which each node is connected to all other nodes, so every pair of distinct nodes is adjacent.

adjacency: In graph representations, adjacency indicates that every two nodes are directly connected; all node pairs in the context are adjacent. The term is used when describing graph types and how nodes are linked.
subgraph: A graph H is called a subgraph of G if every vertex and edge of H belong to G. Thus all vertices and edges of H are contained in G.

vertex set: In graph theory, a vertex set is the set of all vertices of a graph. The notation V(H) ⊆ V(G) indicates that the vertex set of H is a subset of the vertex set of G. Equivalently, every vertex of H is also a vertex of G.
proper subgraph: A proper subgraph is any subgraph other than the whole graph. All other subgraphs are proper subgraphs.
spanning subgraph: a spanning subgraph H of a graph G is a subgraph that has the same vertices as G.

induced subgraph: For a non-empty set S of nodes of a graph G, the induced subgraph G[S] has vertex set S. Two vertices u and v are adjacent in G[S] if and only if they are adjacent in G. Therefore, the induced subgraph retains exactly the edges of G with both endpoints in S, and includes no other edges.
edge set: E(H) and E(G) denote edge sets of graphs H and G, respectively. The relation E(H) \subseteq E(G) indicates that the edge set of H is a subset of the edge set of G.
symmetric matrix: a matrix category distinguished from an asymmetric matrix.

graph sparsity: Graph sparsity is a graph property related to scale/size, referenced alongside density.

covariance matrix: The term appears in the source material.
eigenvalues: The term appears in material on graph properties and matrix representations.

matrix powers: Matrix powers are associated with walks in a graph. The association appears in the topic of graph properties and matrix representations, where the connection is listed as 'Walks (powers of matrices)'.

Datasets for graph classification contain graph-label pairs, such as D = {(G1, y1), ..., (Gn, yn)}. It appears in discussions of GCN training and graph neural network expressiveness.

logistic activation: logistic activation, also known as the sigmoid function, is an activation function used in graph neural network prediction tasks. It is abbreviated as sig in formulas; for example, y = sig[βK + ωK(HK1/N)]. In a graph convolutional network training and optimization pipeline, the output is passed through a sigmoid or softmax function. The notation sig also appears at the start of a formula line in material on inductive/transductive learning and graph classification.

graph neural network: A graph neural network (GNN) is used for graph-based learning and prediction tasks. The graph convolutional network (GCN) is a GNN model. GCN layers perform graph-based aggregation, a GNN hallmark, to compute node embeddings. Each GCN layer is permutation invariant. GCNs support deep, sequential node representation learning.

fixed adjacency matrix: a graph's adjacency matrix A that is fixed, meaning the graph structure does not change during the specific operation being considered. The notation 'A = fixed' appears with graph diagrams to indicate that the connectivity among nodes is held constant for that operation. In the context of graph neural network prediction tasks, such a fixed matrix represents the graph structure and is not altered while the task is performed.

average pooling: In graph neural network prediction tasks, average pooling (also mean pooling) is an operation involving a vector of ones and a scalar N, indicating computation of an average over N values.

node classification: a graph prediction task in which nodes are classified; in graph neural networks, a node is classified from its node embedding. It appears as a graph learning task, including in a GCN training and optimization pipeline and in discussions of inductive vs. transductive learning. It is listed with edge prediction for permutation-invariant/equivariant graph models and cited as an example task for graph isomorphism network expressiveness.

edge prediction: a graph prediction task that predicts the presence of an edge between a pair of nodes. It is also called link prediction. Examples include predicting an edge between nodes 1 and 2, and between nodes m and n. It is mentioned alongside node classification as a graph task.

dot product: A mathematical operation between two vectors that multiplies corresponding components and sums the results. In graph neural networks, it is written as h^(m)T h^(n), representing the dot product between two node embeddings. This value is used as a similarity measure between the embeddings, for example in edge prediction tasks.

binary classification: a prediction task whose output is restricted to two values, such as 0 or 1. In graph tasks, binary classification can be used to predict link existence, with output y^(mn) ∈ {0, 1} indicating whether a link exists.

representation learning: transforms complex features into a space where linear models can work well in the final representation space. In network layers, it is carried out by feature transformations using linear transformations, such as applying the same linear transformation to aggregated nodes. In graph neural networks, representation learning is described as deep sequential node representation learning (embedding), with a Transform step that 'represents it better' and is paired with aggregation (AGG + Transform). The learned representation is a matrix H_K that can be transformed by a weight matrix W for graph-level prediction.

node link prediction: predicting whether a link exists between two nodes. The similarity between nodes u and v can be approximated by the dot product of their vector representations: similarity(u,v) ≈ z_u^T z_v.
graph link prediction: The similarity between two nodes u and v is approximated by the dot product of their embedding vectors, z_u^T z_v.
graph autoencoder: A graph autoencoder is represented as a Graph U-Autoencoder Block. The block appears in the context of encoder-decoder graph neural networks and graph generation.
graph variational autoencoder: Also known as GraphVAE, cited to Simonovsky et al. (2018).

similarity function: In graph neural networks and node embedding, similarity(u,v) is approximated by the dot product of node embeddings z_u^T z_v. The embedding z_u is produced by a function f applied to u, so similarity(u,v) ≈ f(u)^T f(v).
connected nodes: a concept represented by the phrase 'are connected' in the context of graph neural networks and node embedding.
close/similar pairs: pairs (u,v) of nodes that are close or similar. In graph neural networks and node embedding, the term denotes such node pairs.

In graph learning, graph encoders map graph structure to node embeddings, while graph decoders map embeddings back to graphs. Graph generation involves this encoder-decoder mapping, and the central question is how to generate new graphs from learned representations.

graph feature sampling method: a sampling approach in GNN training. Node sampling randomly selects a subset of target nodes.
graph feature generation method: A technique whose aim is to generate the graph adjacency matrix and its node feature matrix in the target domain.
binary classification task: a supervised learning task with two possible class labels. Binary cross-entropy (CE) can be used for classification.

loss function: In optimization, a loss function is defined to optimize. Formalizing a learning task raises the question of how to define it. One presented form is l(w) = 1/n Σ (x̃_i^T w - y_i)^2, the average squared difference between a linear prediction x̃_i^T w and a target y_i. In this form, the loss depends on both the linear prediction and the target value.
matrix multiplication: Given X̃ ∈ R^(n×(d+1)) and w ∈ R^(d+1), their matrix-vector product is ŷ ∈ R^n.

graph neural architecture: A layered design expressed by the recurrence H1 = F[X,A,φ0], H2 = F[H1,A,φ1], H3 = F[H2,A,φ2], ..., HK = F[HK-1,A,φK-1]. The function F transforms the previous representation together with A and a layer-specific parameter φ; the same A appears in every step while φ changes across layers. Each recurrence step corresponds to one layer, so successive representations are generated from input X.

function f: a transformation applied to a feature matrix (X or H), an adjacency matrix A, and a parameter vector φ. It is applied repeatedly: F[X, A, φ0], F[H1, A, φ1], F[H2, A, φ2], ..., F[HK-1, A, φK-1]. This produces hidden states H1, H2, ..., HK-1, using different parameters at each step while the adjacency matrix A remains the same.

GCN layers can be designed and trained as part of a training and optimization pipeline. Efficient algorithms exist for training deep and large graph convolutional networks.
deep neural network: a deep neural network maps or encodes a training sample (node) through a sequence of hidden layers, from hidden layer 1 to hidden layer L.

layer-wise normalization: Layer-wise normalization is associated with a layer-wise normalization and propagation rule. It controls the latent embedding variance.

message passing: a layer-wise feature embedding rule in graph neural networks that updates node embeddings by aggregating feature information from a node itself and its neighboring nodes. Also called feature aggregation and referred to as MPNN, it is a generalized message propagation rule for updating embeddings in a GCN layer; message update rules appear in models such as GIN.

self-loop augmentation: a graph transformation that adds a diagonal enhancement to the adjacency matrix, expressed as Â = A + I. This operation adds the identity matrix to the original adjacency matrix.

output scores: a term labeled 'C output scores' in material on graph-level prediction and inductive capability of graph convolutional networks.

global mean pooling: a term appearing in material on graph-level prediction and the inductive capability of graph convolutional networks. It refers to averaging feature values across elements to produce a fixed-size output.
global max pooling: A pooling approach that appears in the context of graph-level prediction. The term max pooling also appears in the context of graph neural network aggregation.
global sum pooling: a concept referenced in the context of graph-level prediction and the inductive capability of graph convolutional networks.
hierarchical pooling: Hierarchical pooling, also known as DiffPool (2018), is noted in the context of graph-level prediction and inductive capability of GCNs.
operation order: The sequence in which operations are executed. The operation order can change depending on the rationale and target task.

dropout: In graph neural networks, dropout is described as an operation that drops nodes to regularize and increase expressiveness. It appears in discussions of GNN layer operations, including material on aggregation and attention mechanisms. Dropout is also mentioned in the context of GNN training strategies, including batching, sampling strategies, and batch normalization.

batch normalization: In graph neural network (GNN) layer architectures, batch normalization (BN) is an operation that stabilizes optimization and controls embedding variance between layers. Diagrams of GNN layer operations, aggregation/attention mechanisms, and training/batching/sampling strategies include BN, indicating its application across GNN architecture and training contexts.

regularization: Regularization aims to avoid overfitting in neural networks. In GNNs, techniques include dropping nodes to regularize and increase expressiveness, and batch normalization, which injects noise into the training process as a regularizer.
kipf normalization: a normalization approach.
degree matrix: A new GCN layer can be written using the degree matrix.
global embedding aggregation: the process of aggregating embeddings at the graph level.
local embedding aggregation: the process of aggregating embeddings at the node level within a graph.
softmax normalization: a method that normalizes attention weights so they are positive and sum to one; the resulting weights contribute to each output embedding.

attention masking: In graph neural networks, attention masking is a technique that restricts each node's attention to itself and its immediate neighbors. This prevents nodes from attending to distant or unrelated nodes, so aggregation uses local graph structure. The masked attention mechanism focuses the model on relevant connections while ignoring others.
graph attention network: a graph neural network that combines aggregation and attention mechanisms.
graph-based aggregation: a concept associated with graph neural networks (GNNs), identified as the GNN hallmark.
loss objective: A quantity that is optimized when training a model.

parameter update: A parameter update is a rule for revising model parameters during training. The update is expressed as w_{t+1} = w_t - η∇L, where the next parameter vector equals the current parameter vector minus a gradient-based adjustment.
noise in training: updates can be noisy, leading to more erratic convergence behavior.
batch gradient descent: A term named in graph neural network training strategies, appearing in the context of batching considerations.
epoch: An epoch is a complete pass through the entire training dataset.
stability: Stability provides stable error gradients and convergence.

overfitting: Overfitting occurs when a model learns training data too closely and fails to generalize. There is a risk of overfitting when the model is repeatedly exposed to the entire dataset in the same order. To avoid such overfitting, dropout regularization can be applied to a neural network.
convergence: Balanced convergence balances the stable convergence of batch training and the faster fluctuating convergence of stochastic training.
computational efficiency: In GNN training, computational efficiency is characterized by the phrase 'more computationally efficient.' Node sampling reduces computational cost.
gpu acceleration: refers to parallel processing and computing using GPUs.
node embedding computation graph: in GNN training, the term is associated with batching and with layer architecture and dropout regularization.
mini-batch gradient descent: a term used in the context of GNN training strategies and batching.
subgraph sampling: a technique used in mini-batch stochastic gradient descent for training graph neural networks. Mini-batch SGD uses the subgraph that forms the union of the k-hop neighbors.
redundancy: Redundancy occurs between neighboring training nodes. The recursive nature of node-wise sampling brings in redundant computations.
overlap: The term appears as a handwritten annotation in materials titled 'GNN Training Strategies and Batching.'
graph expansion problem: a concept discussed in the context of GNN training strategies and batching.
memory usage: In GNN training, memory usage can increase together with the compute budget. Memory efficiency allows for more efficient memory usage.
disjoint subsets: groups of graph nodes that do not overlap. In GNN training, graph nodes are clustered into such subsets before processing.
exponential time complexity: a computational cost that grows exponentially with the depth of a GCN.
random neighborhood sampling: a term mentioned in the context of graph neural network training strategies and batching.
graph partitioning: A term in GNN training contexts, appearing in material on training strategies and batching, and on sampling strategies and batch normalization.
node sampling: A graph neural network training strategy that randomly selects a subset of target nodes.
information loss: Sampling may result in information loss.
sampling bias: A bias that the sampling process may introduce. In GNN training, sampling strategies may introduce this bias.
ladies: LADIES, also known as layer-dependent importance sampling, is an importance sampling technique attributed to Zou et al. (2019).
graphsaint: GraphSAINT is presented as an example of a sampling strategy in GNN training. The method is attributed to Zeng et al. (2019).
scalability: Scalability allows GNNs to scale to very large graphs.
layer sampling: A sampling strategy used in GNN training.
fastgcn: FastGCN (Chen et al., 2018).
bipartite graph: a graph whose nodes are divided into two sets, with edges only between sets. In GNN training, a bipartite graph is constructed among the nodes between two layers.
empirical mean: The empirical mean, denoted m_h, is a term used in the context of GNN training. It is generally understood as the average of observed data values.
standard deviation: A value denoted s_h is computed.
covariate shift: In machine learning, covariate shift refers to a change in the input distribution. In GNN training, batch normalization is associated with stable covariate shift.

graph neural network layer: A graph neural network (GNN) layer updates node representations by combining the current embedding H_k with graph adjacency A to produce H_{k+1}. This operation is written as H_{k+1} = GraphLayer[H_k, A]. A single GNN layer can take a specified computational form.
attention mechanism: The concept is referred to as 'attention'.
linear layer: A neural network layer that applies a linear transformation to its input. In the absence of a batch normalization layer, dropout is applied directly to the linear layer.

gnn expressiveness: GNN expressiveness, also known as expressive power, is a term used in the context of graph neural networks. It appears in the context of GNN layer architecture and dropout regularization. A question raised is how to maximize the expressiveness of a GNN model. The term is also mentioned in the context of Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) and expressiveness.
training graphs: The term appears in the course materials; the available materials provide no definition.
test graph: A graph used for testing a model.
batching: Batching addresses how to group nodes, including test nodes, when working with graph data. The topic is presented alongside inductive vs. transductive learning and graph classification.

global pooling: an aggregation operation that combines node embeddings into a single graph-level representation. In the illustrated form, it averages node embeddings by multiplying by a vector of ones and dividing by N, the number of nodes. This operation is used in graph classification to produce a representation for the entire graph.
test set inference: In graph classification, the notation h_K^(test) indicates the output representation for test data.

transformation invariance: a property in Euclidean deep learning where a function f is invariant to a transformation t applied to input x exactly when f[t[x]] = f[x], meaning the function's output remains unchanged under the transformation.

node ordering: Node ordering refers to how a graph's nodes are arranged. Different node orderings of the same graph can be denoted by i and j. The notion appears in the context of permutation invariance and equivariance in graph neural networks.

node permutation invariance: a property required of graph neural networks (GNNs) so that learned representations (embeddings) do not depend on the indexing or ordering of graph nodes. This ensures that the same graph, regardless of how its nodes are labeled or permuted, yields the same embedding, making the model's output invariant to node permutations.

node permutation equivariance in gnns: a property of graph neural network computations whereby reordering the nodes of a graph leads to a corresponding reordering of the outputs. Considering all nodes in a graph, GCN computation is permutation equivariant.
node permutation equivariance: a notion presented in the context of permutation invariance and equivariance in graph neural networks.
transformation equivariance: Transformation equivariance appears in the context of Euclidean deep learning.
permutation: A permutation is a bijection from a set to itself.
associativity: Associativity is a property of binary operations where the grouping of operands does not affect the result. In permutations, composition is associative: π ∘ (σ ∘ δ) = (π ∘ σ) ∘ δ.

non-commutativity: a property of composition in which the order of operations affects the result, expressed as π ∘ σ ≠ σ ∘ π. In graph neural networks, this concept appears in the context of permutation invariance and equivariance, indicating that swapping the order of permutations does not generally yield the same outcome.
permutation matrix: A permutation matrix, denoted P, is referenced in the context of permutation invariance and equivariance in graph neural networks.
expressive power of gnn: An expressive GNN model maximizes its node representation capacity by mapping different local neighborhoods to different embeddings.

rooted subtree: A rooted subtree is the structure around a node in a graph. In graph neural networks, computational graphs are identical to rooted subtree structures around each node. Therefore, the computational graph of a node can be viewed as its rooted subtree.

injective aggregation: a neighbor aggregation approach in which, at each layer k, the aggregation function is injective. The function f operates on multisets, and phi is also injective. Injective aggregation is discussed in the context of graph neural network expressive power and the Weisfeiler-Lehman test.
node representation capacity: a graph neural network's capacity to represent nodes in the embedding space. A model can maximize this capacity, and doing so is associated with its expressive power.
node computational graph: A computational structure that models neighborhood aggregation in graph neural networks.
k-hop similarity: a notion of similarity in node local structure.
symmetric neighborhood: A term referenced in the context of the expressive power of graph neural networks and the Weisfeiler-Lehman test.

gin: Short for Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN). GIN is discussed in relation to the expressive power of graph neural networks and the Weisfeiler-Lehman test. A 2019 reference to GIN appears in this context.
dropgnn: DropGNN is mentioned with the year 2021 in the context of the expressive power of graph neural networks and the Weisfeiler-Lehman test.

weisfeiler-lehman graph isomorphism test: The Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test is an effective and computationally efficient test for graph isomorphism. GNNs are at most as powerful as the WL test in distinguishing graph structures.
graph isomorphism problem: The graph isomorphism problem asks whether two graphs are topologically identical.
wl color refinement algorithm: It begins by assigning an initial color. It is associated with the expressive power of graph neural networks and the Weisfeiler-Lehman test.
mean aggregator: an aggregation operator in graph neural networks that fails to distinguish certain graph structures.
max aggregator: an aggregator that, together with mean aggregators, fails to distinguish certain graph structures.
injective hash function: A hash function whose hash table is injective. In an injective hash table, each input maps to a distinct hash value, so collisions are avoided.
multiset: A structure on which a Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) operates.
universal function approximator: a model capable of approximating a wide range of functions to arbitrary accuracy. Multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) are universal function approximators.

aggregation function: An aggregation function combines multiple values into a single value. In the supplied material, the terms 'MAX' and 'MEAN' appear next to a pooling diagram, indicating their role in pooling operations.

generative learning tasks: generative learning tasks are learning tasks formalized in the context of generative graph learning. Their taxonomy includes self-supervised/unsupervised generative GNN tasks and supervised generative GNN tasks.
supervised generative gnn tasks: a generic task category within the formalization of generative learning tasks.
edge feature matrix: In formal notation for learning tasks, an edge feature matrix may be denoted E or E'. It is a matrix that stores features associated with edges.
input graph: The term 'input graph' appears in the formalization of generative learning tasks.

predict and analyze patterns: This task involves predicting and analyzing patterns on given graphs, for example predicting the label of a node or of a graph. It appears under the formalization of generative learning tasks. The task concerns graph-structured data and supports prediction at both the node level and the graph level.
domain a: A domain referenced in the formalization of generative learning tasks.
output label: The output label is a term used in the formalization of generative learning tasks.
multiple output scores: A term used in the context of formalizing generative learning tasks.
gnn aims: A phrase appearing in the context of formalizing generative learning tasks. The intended objectives are not specified.
source graph distribution: a term appearing in the formalization of generative learning tasks.

concept_name: learn the distribution of given graphs
aliases: learn the distribution of given graphs
profile: learn the distribution of given graphs: This task learns the distribution of given graphs and generates more novel graphs. An example is generating a target graph B from a source graph A.
target domain: The phrase 'target domain' appears as a handwritten term in the material; no definition or additional detail is provided.

target graph distribution: a term that occurs in the formalization of generative learning tasks. The available material identifies the phrase but does not define it or specify the distribution to which it refers.
domain b: a domain label appearing in the formalization of generative learning tasks.
adjacency matrix generation: A generative learning task whose aim is to generate only the graph adjacency matrix.
node feature generation: a generative learning task whose aim is to generate the graph adjacency matrix and its node feature matrix in the target domain.

edge feature generation: In generative learning tasks, edge feature generation aims to generate the graph's edge feature matrix in the target domain, alongside the graph adjacency matrix and node feature matrix. This task is part of formalizing generative learning, where the objective is to produce these matrix components for the target graph.
random initialization: a method of assigning starting values by choosing them randomly.
topological attribute initialization: a technique that uses the topological attributes of a given node.
identity vector initialization: an initialization method that uses an identity vector of all ones, [1 1 ... 1].
graph representation learning: in this setting, the target graph has both node and edge features.
generative gnn dimensions: domain, time, and resolution.

multigraph prediction: A generative learning task represented as Source graph -> Target graph 1 ... Target graph n. The notation expresses a mapping from a source graph to target graphs named Target graph 1 through Target graph n. This task is part of the formalization of generative learning tasks.
gnn mapping function: A term that occurs in the context of generative learning tasks formalization.

graph super-resolution: a task that transforms a low-resolution graph into a super-resolved graph. In the context of encoder-decoder GNNs and graph generation, the use of Graph UNet for super-resolving graphs is raised.
brain graph evolution prediction: a task in which a brain graph at baseline t0 is used to predict later brain graphs at time points t2, t3, and t4.
sparsity regularization: In the formalization of generative learning tasks, sparsity regularization appears as the notation 'L2 (sparsity)'. No definition, mechanism, or example is provided.
gnn loss function: A term for the objective function used to train graph neural networks.
loss minimization: In the formalization of generative learning tasks, the notation 'min d1' indicates minimizing a quantity named 'd1'.
utility of graph generation: Graph generation is useful for understanding the graph formation process, identifying abnormal parts of the graph, and predicting new structures.
molecular graph generation: the process of generating new molecular structures, as illustrated by the example of creating a new molecule that cures a certain disease.
density estimation: Density estimation means learning a good model that represents a graph. The model distribution p_model(g; theta) is learned to approximate the data distribution p_data(g).
sampling: In generative graph learning, sampling is the step of drawing a new graph from the model distribution p_model(g). The related term sampled noise also appears in this context.
maximum likelihood estimation: a method that uses maximum likelihood to make the model distribution p_model(g; theta) approximate the data distribution p_data(g).
noise distribution: A noise distribution supplies random samples, for example, a simple noise distribution z_i ~ N(0, 1), where samples are drawn from a standard normal distribution.
deep network function: a function, denoted f(.), that transforms the noise z_i.
unconditional generation: a taxonomy branch in generative graph learning; it is discussed in the context of generative graph neural networks and graph pooling.
one-shot generating: a sub-category under unconditional generation in generative graph learning.
sequential generating: a sub-category under unconditional generation.
node-sequence: a graph generation method categorized under the sequential generating approach in a taxonomy of generative graph learning.
node addition: In generative graph learning, node addition is an operation that adds a new node with two edges.
edge-sequence: A graph generation method categorized under sequential generating in the taxonomy of generative graph learning.
motif-sequence: In the taxonomy of generative graph learning, motif-sequence is a method classified under sequential generating.

rule-sequence: In the taxonomy of generative graph learning, rule-sequence is a method placed under sequential generating. It is listed as one of the approaches for generating graphs sequentially within a broader classification of such methods. The available source does not provide specific operational details or algorithmic mechanisms for rule-sequence; no further technical specifics are given.
edge connection: a graph operation that connects existing nodes to form an edge.
gaussian distribution: A gaussian distribution is represented by the notation N(0, 1).
variational autoencoder: A variational autoencoder has a loss objective. The term NED-VAE appears in the context of encoder-decoder GNNs and graph generation.
latent space: A term used in the context of generative graph neural networks.
gaussian prior: an isotropic Gaussian prior appearing in the context of generative graph neural networks and graph pooling.
reconstruction loss: A loss term also called self-reconstruction loss, appearing in the context of generative graph neural networks and encoder-decoder GNNs.
graphvae: GraphVAE is a method introduced by Simonovsky et al. (2018). It is presented in the context of generative graph neural networks and graph pooling.
node update: Node update (msg) is a term presented in material on generative graph neural networks and graph pooling.

edge update: A term appearing in material on generative graph neural networks and graph pooling. The available source lists the term but provides no definition or explanation of its specific meaning in this context.
kl divergence: a divergence between distributions. KLD is an abbreviation for KL divergence between distributions. The abbreviation KL is also used for this concept.
decoder: A term that appears in material on generative graph neural networks and graph pooling.
graph matching: a concept referred to as approximate graph matching.
softmax: Softmax appears in the context of generative graph neural networks and graph pooling. It can be applied in an edge-wise or a node-wise manner.
argmax: A term that appears in the context of generative graph neural networks and graph pooling. The available material provides the term itself without an accompanying definition or explanation.
element-wise product: a mathematical operation that is denoted in the same context as matrix multiplication, indicating a distinct operation.
projection vector: A projection vector, denoted p, is a trainable vector.
node scores: scores estimating scalar projection values.
encoder-decoder gnns: In the context of generative graph neural networks, Graph UNet (Gao et al., 2019) is presented as an encoder-decoder GNN case study.
node-edge co-transformation: a concept abbreviated as NECT; no definition or further details are provided in the available source.
embedding-based nect: The concept is identified by name only. No definition, role, mechanism, or properties are provided.
editing-based nect: A label appearing in a resource about generative graph neural networks and graph pooling, specifically as the item labeled '(b) Editing-based NECT'.
skip connection: In an encoder block, a skip connection is used to fuse low-level spatial features.
top-k node selection: A concept referenced in the context of generative graph neural networks and graph pooling.
sigmoid activation: The term 'sigmoid' appears in material on generative graph neural networks and graph pooling.

graph unet: A concept referenced as 'Graph UNet (Gao et al., 2019)' and 'g-U-Nets'. It is described as an encoder-decoder GNN case study and appears under 'Generative Graph Neural Networks and Graph Pooling'.
dag-to-dag: A term credited to Kaluza et al. (2018), appearing in the context of generative graph neural networks and graph pooling.
directed acyclic graph: DAG is an abbreviation for directed acyclic graph.
coarsened graph: a graph produced by coarsening; in one example, the resulting coarsened graph contains 4 nodes.
reconstruction: Reconstruction refers to the process of reconstructing the original graph structure.
edge attributes: features associated with the edges of a graph that must be handled when generalizing models such as graph UNet to targets with edge-level information.
graph reconstruction: the transformation G(E,F) -> G'(E',F'), appearing in the context of encoder-decoder GNNs and graph generation.

graph u-autoencoder: A block introduced in the context of encoder-decoder graph neural networks and graph generation. The label appears in this setting, but the block's detailed architecture or functionality is not specified.
ned-vae: NED-VAE (Node Edge Distribution Variational Autoencoder) is a method introduced by Guo et al. (2020).
latent variable: In the context of encoder-decoder GNNs and graph generation, latent variables are represented by the symbols z_f, z_g, and z_e.
mean absolute error: appears in the context of encoder-decoder GNNs and graph generation, computed between At and At~.
eigenvector centrality: a centrality measure. The material contains the notation 'MAE (Eigenvector centrality)'.
degree distribution: the distribution of node degrees across all nodes in a graph.

evaluation metrics: a topic presented under the heading 'Evaluation Metrics for Deep Generative-Based Methods' in material covering encoder-decoder GNNs and graph generation. This heading indicates evaluation metrics are treated as a distinct area of focus when studying deep generative-based methods.
maximum mean discrepancy: maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) is abbreviated as MMD. The only available information is the label 'MMD: Maximum Mean Discrepancy'; no formal definition is provided.

fréchet inception distance: a distance measure between multivariate Gaussian distributions, abbreviated FID. The name is composed of Fréchet, Inception, and Distance. It is defined as the Fréchet Inception Distance between multivariate Gaussian distributions.

graph distribution: In graph generation, the distribution over graphs is represented by the data distribution p_data(g) and the model distribution p_model(g; theta). The notation p_data(g) ~ p_model(g; theta) indicates that the model distribution approximates the data distribution.
